_metadata.description: Hopkins Street corridor project history — timeline and source library
_metadata.note: Timeline events are sourced from public records, journalism, and city documents. Source links point to publicly accessible documents where available. Updated 2026-07-28 with coverage of the revived bike lane plan and the July 28 Council vote; July 2026 details verified against the full text of the SF Chronicle article (Rachel Swan, July 24 2026). The vote entry was added the day of the meeting and records no outcome — update it once the result is on the record.

timeline.title: Pedestrian killed at Hopkins & Monterey
timeline.description: A pedestrian was struck and killed at the intersection of Hopkins Street and Monterey Avenue. The fatality, along with a cyclist death the same year, would trigger the first serious city study of the corridor.

sources.label: Berkeley City Council budget referral, January 2018

timeline.title: Cyclist killed on Sacramento near Hopkins
timeline.description: A cyclist was killed on Sacramento Avenue near Hopkins Street. Two fatalities in one year on the same corridor forced the question onto the city's agenda.

sources.label: Berkeley City Council budget referral, January 2018

timeline.title: City Council budget referral triggers corridor study
timeline.description: Following the two 2017 fatalities, Councilmember Sophie Hahn submitted a budget referral directing staff to study safety improvements on the Hopkins Street corridor using a complete streets approach, integrated with scheduled 2023 repaving.

sources.label: Budget referral document, January 23 2018

timeline.title: Bike East Bay documents 36 collisions on corridor
timeline.description: Bike East Bay reviewed the collision record for the Hopkins corridor and found 36 collisions between 2015 and 2018, with 36% involving a pedestrian or cyclist. The finding was drawn from city staff data.

sources.label: Bike East Bay corridor report (2018), citing city staff data

timeline.title: Vision Zero Action Plan designates Hopkins a High-Injury Street
timeline.description: Berkeley's Vision Zero Action Plan formally designated the Hopkins Street corridor (Sutter to Gilman) as a High-Injury Street — a data-driven classification requiring capital investment. The designation was based on the 2016–2019 collision record.

sources.label: Berkeley Vision Zero Action Plan (2020)

timeline.title: Workshop 1 — Existing conditions and project introduction
timeline.description: The first of four public engagement workshops drew over 100 attendees. Staff presented existing conditions and introduced the complete streets concept. Small group exercises gathered feedback on draft project goals.

sources.label: Workshop 1 summary (PDF)

timeline.title: Workshop 2 — Design options and community feedback
timeline.description: Staff presented three design options (two-way separated bikeway, one-way separated bikeways, buffered bike lanes) and collected community feedback on priorities. Community input showed pedestrian crossing safety, speeding, and cyclist safety as the top three concerns — far above parking improvement, which ranked 9th of 16 issues raised.

sources.label: Workshop 2 Presentation — Transportation and Placemaking Opportunities, March 10 2021

timeline.title: Workshop 3 — Preferred design options
timeline.description: Staff presented preferred design options and placemaking opportunities. Over 700 comments submitted via the Social Pinpoint platform in the five weeks following the workshop.

timeline.title: Workshop 4 — Final segment-by-segment design recommendations
timeline.description: Three virtual community meetings (March 1, 7, and 14) presented the recommended near-term design for each corridor segment. Collision data presented: 18 injury and fatal collisions 2016–2019, 78% involving pedestrians or cyclists. Every collision involving a pedestrian or cyclist resulted in injury or fatality.

sources.label: Workshop 4.1 — Sutter to The Alameda (March 1 2022)
Workshop 4.2 — The Alameda to McGee (March 7 2022)
Workshop 4.3 — McGee to Gilman (March 14 2022)

timeline.title: Council votes 8–1 to approve Hopkins Street design
timeline.description: Berkeley City Council approved the Hopkins Street Safety Project design in an 8–1 vote (Wengraf dissenting). The staff report cited an initial parking removal estimate of 30–35 spaces — a figure that would later be revised upward to 60.

sources.label: Hopkins Corridor Project Conceptual Design — Council Staff Report, May 2022

timeline.title: Parking removal revised upward to ~60 spaces — not disclosed before vote
timeline.description: After the Council vote, it emerged that city staff had revised the parking removal estimate from 30–35 spaces to approximately 60 — but had not disclosed this revision to Council or the public before the May vote. Councilmember Hahn cited this as the basis for requesting reconsideration.

sources.label: "Berkeley to reconsider Hopkins Street bike lane plan" — Berkeleyside, October 2022

timeline.title: Reconsideration motion fails — design reaffirmed
timeline.description: A motion to reconsider the May 2022 vote failed. The Council reaffirmed its approval of the Hopkins Street Safety Project design.

sources.label: Berkeley City Council meeting, October 2022

timeline.title: West of Gilman community meeting — three extension options presented
timeline.description: A virtual community meeting presented three options for extending the protected bikeway west of Gilman Street. City parking surveys found 60% peak occupancy (93 of 155 spaces) in the western area. Options ranged from a 250-foot extension removing 13 spaces (Option 1) to a 3,000-foot extension to Kains Avenue removing 129–132 spaces (Option 3).

sources.label: Hopkins West of Gilman — Virtual Community Meeting, December 12 2022

timeline.title: City indefinitely postpones project — staff shortages cited
timeline.description: City Manager Dee Williams-Ridley postponed the project indefinitely, citing vacancies in the Transportation Division, unresolved safety questions regarding fire access lane widths in the Very High Fire Danger Severity Zone, and the need for further review. The scheduled April 18 Council meeting was canceled.

sources.label: "Hopkins Street bike lane project delayed" — Berkeleyside, April 2023

timeline.title: Transportation Division loses 27% of staff
timeline.description: An exodus of engineers — attributed in part to the political fallout from the Hopkins project — left the Transportation Division with a 27% vacancy rate. Vision Zero implementation stalled citywide for over a year.

sources.label: "What's happening with Measure FF?" — Berkeley Scanner, October 2025

timeline.title: Voters pass Measure FF — street safety parcel tax
timeline.description: Berkeley voters approved Measure FF, a parcel tax dedicated to street safety improvements. Simultaneously, they rejected a competing measure with weaker bicycle and pedestrian commitments. Note: as a compromise during drafting, the Measure FF ballot language explicitly prohibits its funds from being used for bicycle-specific safety improvements on Hopkins Street between McGee and Gilman — the contested commercial strip.

sources.label: "Street safety activists think Berkeley is on verge of big change" — Berkeleyside, June 2025

timeline.title: Fatal collision on California Street near Hopkins
timeline.description: A fatal collision occurred at California Street and Ada Street — one block south of Hopkins — in January 2025, eight years after the two 2017 fatalities that triggered the corridor study, and nearly three years after the Council voted to redesign the street. The Hopkins corridor safety project remained unbuilt at the time.

sources.label: TIMS/SWITRS — Hopkins corridor area collision extract

timeline.title: Project remains unbuilt — nine years after the fatalities
timeline.description: As of early 2026, the Hopkins Street Safety Project has been approved by Council twice and endorsed by ten or more city planning documents, but no construction has begun. Two people died in 2017. A fatal collision occurred one block south of Hopkins in January 2025. The street remains unchanged.

sources.label: City of Berkeley project status page

timeline.title: Two council members propose repaving Hopkins without bike lanes
timeline.description: Councilmembers Kesarwani (D1) and O'Keefe (D5) — the two representatives whose districts include Hopkins — introduced an item to repave the street without the protected bike lane already approved in 2022. Mayor Ishii and Councilmember Humbert co-sponsored. Because Berkeley prohibits digging up newly paved streets for five years, repaving without the lane would lock out safety improvements until at least 2031.

sources.label: "The Hopkins Street battle is back" — Berkeleyside, April 1 2026

timeline.title: National bike press reports fight renewing
timeline.description: Streetsblog San Francisco reported on the renewed conflict, describing the council proposal as "effectively killing the project for the foreseeable future." The story drew regional attention to what had been an internal city process.

sources.label: "Weekend Roundup: Hopkins Fight Renews in Berkeley" — Streetsblog SF, March 13 2026

timeline.title: 100+ supporters rally on Hopkins Street
timeline.description: More than 100 people lined Hopkins Street on a weekday afternoon — ringing bells on their bikes and holding signs including "I wish this was a bike lane" and "I bike and I vote." Walk Bike Berkeley lobbied the Infrastructure Committee against the repaving-without-bike-lanes proposal.

sources.label: "The Hopkins Street battle is back" — Berkeleyside, April 1 2026

timeline.title: Infrastructure Committee recommends paving without protected bike lane
timeline.description: The FITES Infrastructure Committee directed Public Works to develop a paving plan incorporating pedestrian safety features — crosswalks, lighting, traffic calming — but without the protected bike lane. The committee directed staff to return by May 2026 with cost estimates for paving with and without the lane, as part of the FY 2026–28 budget process. Full City Council still decides.

sources.label: Berkeleyside coverage, April 2026

timeline.title: Fire chief shifts position on bike lane emergency access
timeline.description: In an April 2026 memo, city staff indicated that both the one-way and two-way bike path scenarios had an "acceptable" width of 10.5 feet to accommodate an emergency response. Berkeley's fire chief — who had previously voiced concerns that bike lanes could block access for emergency vehicles, one of the stated reasons for the 2023 postponement — no longer opposed the project. Councilmember Kesarwani said the shift changed "what became possible for Hopkins Street."

sources.label: "Why one Berkeley street has become the Bay Area's latest bike-lane battleground" — Rachel Swan, San Francisco Chronicle, July 24 2026
"What's in the revived plan for bike lanes on Hopkins Street" — Berkeleyside, July 27 2026

timeline.title: Berkeley proposes parking meters for the Hopkins commercial strip
timeline.description: Berkeley proposed installing parking meters in the Hopkins Street shopping district and extending meter enforcement to Sundays and evenings. The study and public outreach process would require Council approval before implementation. The same commercial strip whose free parking drove most of the opposition to the bike lane could see paid parking regardless of the bike lane outcome.

sources.label: "Berkeley could extend parking meter hours, hike cost of tickets and permits" — Berkeleyside, May 18 2026

timeline.title: Kesarwani puts forward revived bike lane plan
timeline.description: Councilmember Rashi Kesarwani (D1) — who in January 2026 had co-authored the proposal to repave Hopkins without the bike lane — introduced an updated plan pairing repaving with a revised version of the project shelved in 2023: one-way bike lanes on each side of the street, protected by posts, concrete barriers, or parked cars, stretching nearly a mile from Peralta Avenue (where Hopkins meets the Ohlone Greenway) to the North Branch Library at The Alameda, with painted bike lanes continuing three blocks east to Sutter Street. All street parking would be removed on the 0.4-mile stretch between Monterey and Peralta; east of Monterey, parking would remain on the south side only. The city has not released designs or a parking-impact analysis; interim Public Works Director Wahid Amiri estimated approximately 145 spaces lost in response to a Councilmember inquiry. Kesarwani also called for a "curb management analysis" — possibly adding meters on surrounding blocks — and the plan includes raising the street level at Hopkins and Monterey, where a pedestrian was killed in 2017. Reported costs: roughly $11.2 million for repaving, with the protected bike lanes adding about $3.3 million.

sources.label: "What's in the revived plan for bike lanes on Hopkins Street" — Berkeleyside, July 27 2026
"Why one Berkeley street has become the Bay Area's latest bike-lane battleground" — Rachel Swan, San Francisco Chronicle, July 24 2026

timeline.title: Council takes up the revived plan — third decision on the corridor
timeline.description: The City Council was scheduled to vote on the revived Hopkins bike lane plan at its July 28 regular meeting (6 p.m., BUSD Boardroom, 1231 Addison Street) — the third time the corridor's fate has gone before the full Council since the original 8–1 approval in May 2022. In the days before the vote, anonymous flyers appeared on windshields along the corridor warning that Council would "vote to remove hundreds of parking spaces" and urging residents to speak out. NOTE: this entry was added the day of the meeting and records no outcome; update it once the result is on the public record.

sources.label: City Council Regular Meeting eAgenda, July 28 2026
"Why one Berkeley street has become the Bay Area's latest bike-lane battleground" — Rachel Swan, San Francisco Chronicle, July 24 2026
"This Week: Lake Merritt Ride, Hopkins Vote, Courtyard Urbanism" — Streetsblog SF, July 27 2026
"What's in the revived plan for bike lanes on Hopkins Street" — Berkeleyside, July 27 2026

government.title: Berkeley Vision Zero Action Plan
government.summary: Formal city policy committing to zero traffic fatalities. Designated Hopkins Street (Sutter to Gilman) a High-Injury Street based on the 2016–2019 collision record. Requires capital investment on designated corridors.
key_facts: Hopkins corridor designated High-Injury Street
Data period: 2016–2019 (contested by opposition as anomalous — see full time series in collision analysis)
Target: zero traffic fatalities by 2028

government.title: Hopkins Street Safety Project — Council Staff Report
government.summary: Staff report recommending Council approval of the Hopkins Street Safety Project design. Included design concept, cost estimate, and the initial parking impact figure of 30–35 spaces. Approved 8–1.
key_facts: 8–1 Council approval, May 2022
Initial parking estimate: 30–35 spaces (later revised to ~60, not disclosed before vote)
Design includes protected bike lanes, Sutter to Gilman

government.title: Reconsideration of Hopkins Corridor Plan in Light of Newly Available Material Information — Action Calendar Item 23
government.organization: City of Berkeley (Councilmember Sophie Hahn, author; Councilmember Susan Wengraf, co-sponsor)
government.summary: The reconsideration motion filed by Councilmember Hahn after the disclosure that parking loss estimates had been revised from 30–35 to 60 spaces without informing Council before the May vote. Attachment A (pages 10–12) is the withheld parking count spreadsheet, prepared mid-April 2022. The document quotes a Councilmember asking about the count at the May 10 meeting and being told "We can do a count. I don't have the exact number" — when the count already existed. Council ultimately voted unanimously to continue the project while ordering additional study of the McGee-to-Gilman segment.
key_facts: Parking count spreadsheet (Attachment A) prepared mid-April 2022 — not disclosed before May 10 vote
60 spaces total: 39 in the contested commercial area (McGee to Gilman), 21 across the residential blocks
Gilman to Monterey: all 35 existing spaces removed; Monterey to McGee: 4 of 10 spaces
Document confirms staff verbally claimed parking loss was ~30–35 spaces in public meetings
Hahn motion: proceed with Sutter–McGee segment, pause McGee–Gilman pending independent study, K for study
Council vote: unanimous to continue project with additional study ordered

government.title: Workshop 2 — Transportation and Placemaking Opportunities
government.summary: Second public workshop presenting three design options and collecting community feedback. Community prioritization exercise showed pedestrian crossing safety, speeding, and cyclist safety as the top concerns — parking improvement ranked 9th of 16 issues. Also contains the all-collisions figure: 36 collisions 2015-2018, 36% involving cyclists or pedestrians.

Community 3rd concern: Cyclist Safety/Facilities (~17 mentions)

Parking retention for Sonoma-McGee: all options = 35-40% retained

Parking-protected bike lane southbound, Class II lane northbound

journalism.title: What's in the revived plan for bike lanes on Hopkins Street
journalism.summary: Detailed preview of the plan before Council on July 28, 2026. Kesarwani — a January co-author of the repave-without-lanes item — instead put forward a version of the shelved bike lane project. Includes the Public Works parking estimate, segment-level parking changes, costs, and the Fire Department's reversal on emergency access.

Initial Public Works estimate: 145 parking spaces removed
All street parking removed Monterey to Peralta (0.4 mi); south-side-only parking east of Monterey
Raised street level at Hopkins/Monterey — site of the 2017 pedestrian fatality
Reported costs: ~$11.2M repaving; protected bike lanes add ~$3.3M
Fire Department report: bike lane would not significantly impede emergency response — reversal from 2023

journalism.title: Why one Berkeley street has become the Bay Area's latest bike-lane battleground
journalism.author: Rachel Swan
journalism.summary: July 24, 2026 feature ahead of the July 28 Council vote. Details the revived plan: one-way protected lanes on each side (posts, concrete barriers, or parked cars), nearly a mile from Peralta/Ohlone Greenway to the North Branch Library at The Alameda, painted lanes continuing three blocks east to Sutter. Reports that the city has not released designs or a parking-impact analysis — the ~145-space figure came from interim Public Works Director Wahid Amiri in response to Councilmember O'Keefe's inquiry. Frames Hopkins alongside Telegraph Avenue (Oakland), Richmond Street (El Cerrito), and Valencia Street (San Francisco), with a largely generational divide: older, car-dependent homeowners in Thousand Oaks versus young families in Westbrae.
key_facts: By Rachel Swan, San Francisco Chronicle, July 24 2026 (link is a Yahoo News syndication of the article)
City has not released designs or calculated parking loss; no parking-impact analysis conducted yet
~145 spaces: informal estimate by interim Public Works Director Wahid Amiri, in email to Councilmember O'Keefe
Protected lanes: Peralta to The Alameda (~1 mile); painted lanes three blocks east to Sutter
April 2026 staff memo: 10.5-ft width "acceptable" for emergency response in both one-way and two-way scenarios; fire chief no longer opposed
Previous design (two-way track on south side) "left for dead" in 2023
Opposition group: Friends of Hopkins Street (aka Save Hopkins), organized by Donna DeDiemar
Anonymous flyers on windshields urged residents to oppose parking removal at the July 28 vote
Fight has spanned two mayoral administrations and at least one internal City Hall investigation

opposition.title: Save Hopkins / Friends of Hopkins Street — opposition materials
opposition.organization: Friends of Hopkins Street (aka Save Hopkins)
opposition.summary: The primary opposition group, formed around the parking removal concern and organized by Donna DeDiemar (per SF Chronicle, July 2026). Their central arguments: (1) the revised parking estimate (60 spaces) was not disclosed before the 2022 Council vote; (2) the 2016–2019 designation period was an anomaly; (3) parking loss would harm local businesses and residents who depend on cars, including seniors and people with disabilities. Ahead of the July 28, 2026 vote, DeDiemar conducted her own parking counts on the corridor, citing the absence of released city designs. These arguments are engaged directly in the data analysis — see the collision time series and the data integrity notes.
key_facts: Core argument: undisclosed parking revision undermines vote legitimacy
Claims 2016–2019 was an anomalous period — addressed by full TIMS time series
Raises legitimate concerns about business impact and accessibility for seniors
2026: argues no alternative to the bike lane design has been seriously considered
